item.title: Defending SaaS-based CRM platforms against OAuth abuse campaigns
item.description: Northwind describes an OAuth abuse campaign affecting SaaS CRM platforms.
item.content:encoded:
In a series of campaigns observed between mid-2025 and mid-2026, Northwind Security Research identified threat actor activity abusing trusted OAuth relationships between third-party applications and connected SaaS platforms, rather than relying on stolen credentials.

Northwind observed this activity across many tenants spanning multiple industries, including financial services, healthcare, retail, and manufacturing. Once an OAuth application was approved, the actor systematically queried and exfiltrated customer relationship management (CRM) records at scale, and in several cases established persistent access that survived password resets and routine remediation.

Northwind assesses this activity as a high-impact risk to affected organizations given the scale, persistence, and sensitivity of the exfiltrated data. These findings reinforce the importance of monitoring OAuth-connected applications, validating third-party integrations, and reviewing application permission configurations on an ongoing basis.

The following section describes the attack chain in additional technical detail, covering the initial access technique, the sequence of API calls used to enumerate available objects, and the pattern of export requests observed across affected tenants.

Session tokens issued to the malicious OAuth application were reused across subsequent requests, allowing the actor to avoid triggering repeated re-authentication prompts that might otherwise have drawn administrator attention to the connected application.

Defenders reviewing audit logs should expect to see a burst of read-heavy API activity shortly after a new OAuth application is granted consent, often followed by large sequential export operations targeting CRM object types such as accounts, contacts, and case records.

In several observed cases, the exported data volume substantially exceeded what would be expected from ordinary integration usage, providing a further behavioral signal that audit tooling can flag independently of any single indicator of compromise.

More recently, in June 2026, a separate incident affecting a mid-market technology vendor showed the same tradecraft: a newly registered OAuth application obtained broad CRM read and export scopes and exfiltrated data before being revoked.

Because this activity relies on legitimate OAuth consent grants rather than stolen credentials, it evades traditional authentication-based detections such as failed-login monitoring or impossible-travel alerting; investigators consistently found the resulting application activity indistinguishable from ordinary usage until export volumes were reviewed directly.

Additional indicators of compromise and a mapping to relevant MITRE ATT&CK techniques are provided in the appendix below for defenders who wish to hunt for this activity in their own environments.

Recommended detection queries for the SaaS platforms discussed above are maintained separately and updated as new variants of this tradecraft are identified across the observed campaigns.

This research was compiled with contributions from multiple members of the Northwind Security Research team, and reflects analysis of telemetry collected across several unrelated customer environments over the observation period described above.

Organizations that identify similar activity in their own environments are encouraged to revoke the offending OAuth application immediately, rotate any credentials it may have accessed, and review export logs for the affected time window.
